title: Act I, Scene V

teacherSummary.text: Lady Macbeth reads Macbeth's letter about the prophecies and fears his nature is 'too full o' the milk of human kindness.' Hearing that Duncan will stay the night, she calls on spirits to 'unsex me here' and fill her with cruelty, and asks thick night to hide her knife. Macbeth arrives; she tells him to 'look like the innocent flower, but be the serpent under't' and to leave the business to her.

context.history: Early modern ideas of gender linked women with pity and nursing and men with violence; Lady Macbeth's invocation deliberately reverses those expectations. Calling on spirits echoed what the witchcraft laws punished.

significance: Lady Macbeth's soliloquy is one of the play's great speeches: she sees ambition as requiring the suppression of feeling and of gender itself. Her flower and serpent image restates 'fair is foul' as a plan.
discussionQuestions: Is it ever right to hide your true feelings to get something you want?

anchorPassages.note: She diagnoses his ambition without the illness that should attend it.
anchorPassages.text:
Glamis thou art, and Cawdor; and shalt be
What thou art promised: yet do I fear thy nature;
It is too full o’ the milk of human kindness
To catch the nearest way: thou wouldst be great;
Art not without ambition, but without
The illness should attend it: what thou wouldst highly,
That wouldst thou holily; wouldst not play false,
And yet wouldst wrongly win: thou’ldst have, great Glamis,
That which cries “Thus thou must do, if thou have it;
And that which rather thou dost fear to do
Than wishest should be undone.” Hie thee hither,
That I may pour my spirits in thine ear;
And chastise with the valour of my tongue
All that impedes thee from the golden round,
Which fate and metaphysical aid doth seem
To have thee crown’d withal.

weDoAnswers: Milk is nurturing; she wants to replace it with gall (bitterness). She advises: "look like the innocent flower, / But be the serpent under't": appearance and reality.
analysis.weDoWords: “Innocent flower” and “serpent” stand out. The flower is the welcoming face and the serpent the danger hidden beneath it, so Lady Macbeth teaches her husband to deceive.
analysis.weDoQ2: Lady Macbeth takes charge by teaching the deception, so the line shows her power coming from cunning and control, the qualities she has asked the spirits to give her in place of tenderness.

words.sentence:
He that’s coming
Must be provided for: and you shall put
This night’s great business into my dispatch;
Which shall to all our nights and days to come
Give solely sovereign sway and masterdom.

Come to my woman’s breasts,
And take my milk for gall, you murdering ministers,
Wherever in your sightless substances
You wait on nature’s mischief!

segments.script: Early modern ideas of gender linked women with pity and nursing and men with violence; Lady Macbeth's invocation deliberately reverses those expectations. Calling on spirits echoed what the witchcraft laws punished. Lady Macbeth's soliloquy is one of the play's great speeches: she sees ambition as requiring the suppression of feeling and of gender itself. Her flower and serpent image restates 'fair is foul' as a plan. Characterization: Lady Macbeth reads Macbeth's letter, fears his nature is "too full o' the milk of human kindness," and calls on spirits to "unsex me here." Imagery: Milk vs. gall, light vs. "thick night": the imagery of nurturing turned to poison. Soliloquy: Her speeches reveal resolve and fear of her own pity. Watch for the prophecies: The Witches' riddling prophecies: notice how each promise shapes what Macbeth hopes, fears and does next.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “It is too full o’ the milk of human kindness / To catch the nearest way” slowly and put it in my own words: Reading his letter, Lady Macbeth fears Macbeth is too full of the milk of human kindness to take the quickest path to the crown. Next, craft. I notice the image of milk, nourishment associated with mothers and gentleness. The strongest word is “kindness”: it means natural human feeling, which she sees as weakness. Then, effect. What does Lady Macbeth fear about her husband's nature? My answer: She believes Macbeth is too gentle to murder; she resolves to push him, and later calls on spirits to "unsex" her, rejecting her own nurturing nature.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Annotate the scene for characterization, imagery (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this scene suggest about Lady Macbeth's resolve? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how Act I, Scene V develops the idea of Lady Macbeth's resolve. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of imagery and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: Lady Macbeth believes that to seize power she must destroy her own capacity for pity. When the text says “Come, you spirits / That tend on mortal thoughts, unsex me here” (Act I, Scene V, lines 397–398), it shows this directly. She fears her husband is "too full o' the milk of human kindness" and calls on spirits to "unsex me here," linking kindness to womanhood and cruelty to power.
